strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored empirical question: the geometric relationship between initial Gaussian noise, generated samples, and DDIM-inverted latents, which matters for a large body of diffusion-based editing work.

The analysis is systematic and multi-faceted: pixel correlation statistics (Table 1), angle/triangle geometry between noise, sample, and latent (Figure 2), distance-to-interpolation analysis (Figure 3), and ablations over the number of diffusion steps T (Tables 3-5).

The training-dynamics experiments (Figures 4, 5, 6, 7) are a genuine value-add, showing that the noise-to-sample mapping and its spatial properties are established very early in training and remain stable, with multiple checkpoints and multiple seeds.
Experiments span three different model/dataset combinations (pixel-space DDPMs on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 64x64, and an LDM on CelebA), which increases the credibility of the qualitative conclusions.
The appendix is thorough, including failure-mode analysis of the noise-to-sample assignment (attractor images with low pixel variance) that explains when the L2-based assignment breaks down.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core observations are largely confirmatory of known results. The non-Gaussianity of DDIM inversion latents is already acknowledged in Garibi et al. (2024), Parmar et al. (2023), and Huberman-Spiegelglas et al. (2024), and the noise-to-image mapping is analyzed in Khrulkov & Oseledets (2022), Kadkhodaie et al. (2024), and Zhang et al. (2024). The paper incrementally extends these findings rather than providing new theory or new capability.

The paper is purely empirical, with no theoretical analysis of the inversion approximation error, no formal characterization of the latent distribution, and no derivation supporting the claimed geometric relations (e.g., why the latent angle is always obtuse).

Lack of actionable consequences: the findings are not translated into a method, improvement, or concrete guideline (e.g., better inversion, editing, or sampling). The practical significance for the inversion/editing community remains unclear beyond 'be careful when reasoning about latents'.

Scope concerns: all experiments use unconditional models on relatively small datasets; text-to-image models with classifier-free guidance, where inversion error is most consequential and where most editing applications live, are only discussed but not evaluated.

The 'triangle' angle analysis projects high-dimensional relationships into a 2D figure; the interpretation that latents lie 'along the trajectory' is suggestive rather than rigorously established (e.g., no quantitative measure of proximity to the actual sampling trajectory beyond one interpolation-distance heatmap).

Some claims are over-stated relative to evidence, e.g., 'creating a gap between the diffusion models' theory and practice' and 'far-reaching consequences' are asserted without demonstrating concrete downstream failures.
Writing and presentation issues remain (e.g., 'staring noise' typo in the abstract, awkward phrasing), and Table 2 lacks the LDM T=4000 entry without explanation.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a logical progression from characterizing DDIM inversion error (Section 4.2-4.3) to analyzing noise-to-sample mappings during training (Section 4.4).

The empirical analysis is reasonably thorough for what it attempts: three models (CIFAR-10, ImageNet 64x64, LDM CelebA), multiple evaluation metrics (angles, L2 distances, Pearson correlations, CKA/SSIM/SVCCA/DINO alignments), ablations on the number of diffusion steps T (Appendix A.2), and multiple training seeds for fine-tuning experiments.

Several observations are potentially useful to practitioners, e.g., that DDIM latents are geometrically located between the true noise and the image along the sampling trajectory, and that noise-to-image mappings stabilize very early in training.
The appendix provides helpful supporting material, including qualitative failure modes (low-variance 'attracting' samples in Appendix A.1) and additional qualitative training-dynamics visualizations.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the central observations are largely confirmatory. That DDIM inversion latents are not Gaussian and contain image structure is already noted in prior work the paper itself cites (Garibi et al. 2024, Parmar et al. 2023, Hong et al. 2024, Huberman-Spiegelglas et al. 2024); that diffusion models converge to consistent noise-to-image mappings is established by Khrulkov & Oseledets (2022), Kadkhodaie et al. (2024), and Zhang et al. (2024). The paper's contributions are incremental refinements and re-measurements of known phenomena.

No method, algorithm, theory, or actionable outcome follows from the analysis. The paper identifies that reverse DDIM latents are not noise and that L2 distance can match noises to samples, but it does not propose any fix, explain the mechanism formally, or demonstrate downstream utility (e.g., improved editing, better inversion, improved training efficiency). The 'consequences' discussed (Section 4.3) remain vague and speculative.

The analysis is purely geometric/empirical with no theoretical grounding. Claims like 'latents are located along the trajectory xt' rest on averaged angles and 2D triangle visualizations; a simple theoretical treatment of the inversion error (the approximation in Eq. 4) could explain the observed geometry, but none is attempted.

Experiments are restricted to unconditional models at modest resolutions (32x32, 64x64, CelebA), while many of the motivating applications (text-to-image editing) are conditional models with classifier-free guidance - precisely the setting where inversion error is worst (as acknowledged on page 2). This limits the relevance and generality of the findings.

Some conclusions feel weak or trivially expected: that longer training does not improve DDIM inversion accuracy, and that image content stabilizes early in training while high-frequency detail improves later, are not surprising given how the DDPM training objective is dominated by low-noise levels early on. The connection to a principled account of which timesteps dominate is not explored.

Significance is questionable: for a top-tier venue, the paper offers observational insights without clear impact on any sub-area. There is no demonstration that the identified 'gap between theory and practice' leads to spurious discoveries in any real workflow, despite this being stated as motivation.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: no code release is mentioned, and some experimental details (e.g., which pretrained checkpoints are used, the LDM configuration, how samples are generated from 'the same fixed noise' across checkpoints) are underspecified.

Writing quality is uneven in places, including typos ('staring noise'), an inconsistent duplicate Kadkhodaie reference (2023 vs. 2024), and some figures (e.g., Figure 2's 'most probable relation' triangles) whose construction and interpretation require more careful justification than given.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly written empirical study of an important practical gap in diffusion models: the discrepancy between the theoretical Gaussian prior and the latents actually produced by DDIM inversion

Comprehensive experimental design across three models (DDPM CIFAR-10, DDPM ImageNet 64x64, LDM CelebA), with reasonable sample sizes (N=1000-2048) and multiple random seeds for fine-tuning experiments

The geometric 'triangle' analysis (Figure 2) and trajectory-to-interpolation distance analysis (Figure 3) provide an intuitive and novel way to localize where DDIM latents actually sit relative to the noise and the sampling trajectory

The longitudinal training analysis (Figures 4-7) is a genuinely interesting contribution, showing that noise-to-image mappings stabilize very early in training and that prolonged training only refines high-frequency detail
The noise-attracting-samples analysis in the appendix (low-variance images attracting most noises) is a nice mechanistic insight into when L2-based noise assignment fails
Good use of diverse verification metrics (Pearson correlations, angle/L2 geometry, CKA/SSIM/SVCCA/DINO alignment) to triangulate the same conclusions
weaknesses: The paper is purely observational: all main findings are already suspected or partially established in prior work (non-Gaussian inversion latents was noted by Garibi et al., Parmar et al., Hong et al.; noise-to-image mapping consistency by Khrulkov & Oseledets, Zhang et al.). The delta over these works is incremental quantification rather than new insight

No theoretical explanation is offered for any of the central phenomena. Why are inverted latents non-Gaussian? Why does the noise-to-image mapping freeze in early training? The paper documents but does not explain, which limits its significance and impact

No actionable takeaway: the findings do not lead to an improved inversion method, better editing procedure, or practical guidance beyond 'DDIM inversion is inaccurate' — practitioners already knew this, which is why exact-inversion methods exist

Evaluation is limited to unconditional, relatively small-scale models (CIFAR-10, 64x64 ImageNet, CelebA LDM). The most relevant setting for inversion techniques — conditional text-to-image models with classifier-free guidance, where inversion error is known to be worst — is not studied

Some analyses feel superficial: e.g., the claim that improving generative quality does not improve inversion accuracy is based on angle/distance convergence alone; no reconstruction quality metrics (LPIPS, PSNR of DDIM reconstruction vs. training time) are reported

The L2-based noise assignment result (Table 2) is largely a sanity check with a known failure mode (low-variance samples), and the sample size of 1000 for the assignment experiments is small relative to the effect being estimated

Figures 2's 'most probable relation' triangles average angles across samples in 2D, which is a somewhat informal visualization; error distributions and variability are underexplored relative to the strong conclusions drawn

strengths: The paper provides a thorough, well-structured empirical analysis of the divergence between DDIM inversion latents and Gaussian noise, organized around clearly posed research questions (existence of divergence, spatial location, origin, and practical consequences).

The evaluation is unusually broad for an analysis paper: six diverse diffusion models (ADM-32/64/256, LDM, DiT, Deepfloyd IF) spanning pixel and latent spaces, multiple datasets, and both unconditional and conditional settings, with quantified evidence (Pearson correlations, variance ratios, per-pixel error decomposition, KL divergence) rather than only qualitative illustrations.

The attribution of the divergence to higher noise-prediction approximation error in plain image regions during the first ~10% of inversion steps is a genuinely new and interesting finding, supported by a carefully designed protocol (Appendix D) that isolates per-timestep errors.

The practical consequences section (interpolation quality via FID/Precision/Recall, reduced edit diversity measured with DreamSim/LPIPS/SSIM/DINO, asymmetric noise-to-sample vs. latent-to-sample mapping) convincingly demonstrates downstream impact, making the analysis relevant to a large body of editing and interpolation work.

The mitigation experiment (replacing DM predictions with ground-truth ones in the first 3-5 inversion steps) validates the causal claim that early-step errors drive the phenomenon, and the released code supports reproducibility.
The supplementary material (mask construction, most-probable-triangle analysis, training-dynamics experiments) is detailed and adds depth to the main claims.
weaknesses: The core observation that DDIM inversion latents deviate from Gaussian noise is already documented in prior work (the authors themselves cite Parmar et al., Garibi et al., etc. and 'confirm existing claims'); the novelty lies mainly in the plain-region analysis and first-step attribution, which narrows the delta over the state of the art.

The paper is purely analytical and proposes no new method or fix; the mitigation requires access to ground-truth diffusion predictions from the backward process, which is unavailable for real image editing scenarios, limiting practical utility of the main actionable conclusion.

Some analyses lack theoretical grounding - the phenomenon is well explained intuitively (local linearity assumption, flat prediction in smooth regions) but no formal or quantitative model of the error accumulation is provided; the triangle-geometry analysis (Sec 3.3) is somewhat ad hoc and its interpretation is qualitative.

The experiments rely mostly on generated images and relatively small sample sizes for some analyses (e.g., N=4000 or 20k samples); results on real (non-synthetic) images, which is the setting most editing applications care about, are underexplored.

The related-work positioning, while extensive, does not sharply delineate which findings are confirmatory versus novel; some readers may view a substantial part of the paper as an in-depth extension of known results.

No comparison against or discussion of newer exact/approximate inversion techniques (e.g., EDICT, DPM-Solver-based inversion) as baselines that could sidestep the studied problem, which would contextualize the significance of the DDIM-specific findings.

strengths: The paper is well-organized around four clear research questions, moving systematically from observation (latents deviate from Gaussian noise) to explanation (approximation error concentrated in plain image regions and in the first inversion steps) to consequences (worse interpolation, editing diversity, and ill-defined noise-to-sample mapping).

The empirical study is broad, covering six different diffusion models across pixel and latent spaces, unconditional and conditional settings, with reasonably large sample sizes (e.g., 10,000 samples for correlation and variance analyses).

Several analyses are thoughtful and go beyond prior observations: the per-pixel plain/non-plain error breakdown (Tab. 5, Fig. 4), the noise-image-latent triangle geometry (Sec. 3.3), the step-wise localization of inversion error (Tab. 6), and the training-time analysis in Appendix G showing that noise-to-image mappings are established early in training.

The quantitative ablation in Sec. 5 (replacing early inversion predictions with ground-truth predictions) provides a clean causal check that the first ~10% of inversion steps drive most of the divergence, which is a useful diagnostic finding.
Code is reportedly available, and the appendix contains substantial methodological detail (masking thresholds, error measurement protocol, assignment experiments), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the central finding. The paper itself acknowledges that prior works (Parmar et al. [35], Garibi et al. [10], Wallace et al. [49], Hong et al. [16]) already observed that DDIM inversion latents deviate from Gaussian white noise and cause poor editability. The main new contributions — attributing the deviation to plain image regions and to the first inversion steps — are empirical refinements of a known phenomenon rather than a fundamentally new insight.

The paper is almost entirely empirical. There is no theoretical analysis of why the local-linearity approximation error is larger for smooth image regions, which limits the depth and generality of the explanation. A formal or at least semi-analytic treatment (e.g., relating error to local Lipschitz constants of the score network) would substantially strengthen the contribution.

The proposed mitigation is not practical. The experiments in Sec. 5 replace early inversion predictions with 'ground truth' diffusion predictions obtained from the backward process — an oracle unavailable in real applications. The paper thus identifies and confirms the problem but offers no usable fix (e.g., no comparison against existing improved inversion methods such as Reno [10], exact inversion [49], or numerical approaches [29]), which weakens the significance of the final section.

Some experimental choices limit realism: CFG is disabled (w = 1) despite the authors noting that CFG is known to worsen inversion error [32], and only T = 50/100 steps are used. Since practical editing pipelines operate with strong guidance and varying step counts, the consequences reported in Sec. 4 may not reflect deployed behavior.

Significance is questionable for a top-tier venue. The practical takeaways are largely 'DDIM inversion latents are imperfect and this matters for editing/interpolation' — a conclusion many practitioners already act on by using improved inversion variants. The paper does not demonstrate that its finer-grained understanding changes any downstream decision or enables a better method.

Some analyses feel under-motivated or tangential (e.g., the closest-l2 assignment experiments in Sec. 4.3 and Appendix E, and the extensive training-time studies in Appendix G), which dilutes the narrative without adding much to the core claims.

strengths: Thorough and well-organized empirical study across six diverse diffusion models (pixel-space ADM/IF and latent-space LDM/DiT), covering multiple datasets, resolutions, and conditioning types, which strengthens the generality of the findings.

The analysis goes beyond confirming known observations: it localizes the divergence of DDIM latents to plain/smooth image regions (Tables 2, 5, Fig. 2), attributes it to the approximation error in the first inversion steps (Fig. 4, Table 6), and quantifies downstream consequences for interpolation, editing diversity, and noise-to-sample mapping (Tables 7, 8, Fig. 5, 6).

The diagnostic experiment in Sec. 5 that replaces diffusion model predictions with ground-truth predictions for the first k inversion steps provides a clean causal validation of the claimed origin of the divergence, and the training-time analysis in Appendix G adds useful insight into when noise-image mappings are established.

Clear paper structure built around four research questions, with conclusions per section; the paper is easy to follow and the methodology details (masks, error computation, triangle analysis) are well documented in the appendix.
Code is stated to be available, and experiments use standard checkpoints, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the central observation: that DDIM inversion latents deviate from Gaussian white noise and that this is due to inversion approximation error has already been noted in prior works (Parmar et al., Garibi et al./Renoise, Hong et al., Wallace et al.), which the authors themselves acknowledge. The paper mostly refines and localizes a known phenomenon rather than establishing a new one.

No actionable method or solution is proposed. The main mitigation experiment (replacing DM predictions with ground-truth predictions from the denoising trajectory) is only feasible for synthetic images where intermediate sampling predictions are available; it cannot be applied to real-image inversion, which is the primary practical setting for editing. Consequently, the practical impact of the analysis is limited to motivating future work.

The analysis is entirely empirical; there is no theoretical treatment of why smooth regions induce larger approximation errors (e.g., relating to local Lipschitz behavior of the score in low-variance areas), which would significantly strengthen the contribution.

Several conclusions feel anticipated or incremental: e.g., that latent interpolations are worse than noise interpolations, and that latents sit 'between' noise and images, are largely expected given the inversion construction; the 'triangle' analysis (Sec. 3.3) is descriptive rather than predictive.

Evaluation of consequences relies on proxy metrics (FID/Recall on interpolations, diversity metrics on edits) without a user study or downstream task benchmarks, making the practical significance of the quality degradation harder to gauge.

Experiments are restricted to T=50 or 100 steps and w=1 (CFG disabled); given that real applications use few steps and large guidance scales, the analyzed regime may understate or distort the practical severity of the issue.

strengths: Well-structured, systematic empirical analysis of the DDIM inversion process: the paper poses four clear research questions and answers each with dedicated experiments (correlations, geometric location of latents, origin of divergence, practical consequences).
Broad experimental coverage across six diffusion models (pixel and latent space, conditional and unconditional, U-Net and DiT), which strengthens the generality of the findings.

The key finding — that the inversion approximation error is concentrated in the early steps and disproportionately affects plain/smooth image regions — is a genuinely new, well-supported insight that extends prior work (Lee et al., Lin et al.) and explains previously observed but unexplained phenomena.

The proposed fix is simple, well-motivated by the analysis, and validated quantitatively (correlations, PNG compression, FID/recall of interpolations, diversity and CLIP-T of edits) and qualitatively (stochastic editing, interpolation).

Extensive appendices with ablations (impact of number of steps up to T=1000, training-time dynamics, noise-to-image mapping analysis, failure cases), limitations, compute resources, and pseudocode, supporting reproducibility and honest reporting.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: the fact that DDIM latents deviate from Gaussian noise and are less editable was already reported by Parmar et al., Garibi et al. (Renoise), and others; the main contribution is a more detailed empirical explanation rather than a fundamentally new method or theory.

The proposed solution (replacing early inversion steps with forward diffusion) is very simple and close in spirit to existing ideas (SDEdit-style noising; Renoise's correlation-penalizing regularization), and the paper does not compare against these existing inversion-improvement methods (e.g., Renoise, Null-text Inversion, negative-prompt inversion) on the same tasks.

All experiments disable classifier-free guidance (w=1) for analytical clarity, which limits direct relevance to the most common practical setting (Stable Diffusion-style text-to-image editing with CFG); no results on Stable Diffusion are provided despite the widespread use of DDIM inversion there.

The analysis is entirely empirical — there is no theoretical grounding for why smooth regions produce larger prediction errors or why forward diffusion in early steps preserves reconstruction, leaving some causal claims supported only by correlations.

Some evaluation is narrow: editing experiments use only DiT and IF with fixed T=50, interpolation analysis relies on FID-10k which is a coarse proxy, and the CelebA LDM case shows the phenomenon may not generalize uniformly (as acknowledged in the limitations).

strengths: Comprehensive empirical analysis of DDIM inversion across six different diffusion models (pixel and latent space, conditional and unconditional), which strengthens the generality of the observations.

The paper goes beyond the previously reported observation that DDIM latents are correlated by providing a mechanistic explanation: the approximation error is spatially concentrated in smooth/plain regions and dominates the first inversion steps (tables 5-6, fig. 4), which is a genuinely useful new insight.

The proposed fix (replacing the first ~4% of inversion steps with forward diffusion) is simple, cheap (~3.9% faster), well-motivated by the analysis, and supported by multiple evaluations (correlation metrics, FID/recall along interpolation paths, edit diversity and CLIP alignment).

Honest limitations section, failure cases, ablations over the number of steps (appendix E, showing the effect persists even at T=1000), and detailed appendices including pseudocode and methodology for the error measurements.
The training-dynamics analysis (appendix M) showing noise-image-latent relations are established early in training is an interesting side contribution.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core phenomenon (DDIM latents deviate from Gaussian noise, causing poor editability) is already established in prior work (Parmar et al., Garibi et al./Renoise), which the paper itself acknowledges. The delta is the spatial attribution to plain regions, which, while interesting, is an incremental refinement of a known result.

The proposed solution, though effective, is quite close to a trivially expected remedy given the diagnosis (replace error-prone early steps with forward noising, in the spirit of SDEdit-style stochasticity). Its simplicity is a practical virtue but reduces the technical contribution.

Missing comparison against stronger inversion baselines: the editing/interpolation improvements of the proposed method are never benchmarked against existing inversion techniques designed to improve editability (e.g., Null-text inversion, Renoise, exact inversion methods, DDPM noise space of Huberman-Spiegelglas et al.). It remains unclear how the simple fix compares in practice to these established methods.

Evaluation is largely performed on model-generated images rather than real images, which weakens the relevance of the claims for the main use case of inversion (real image editing); real-image experiments are relegated to a qualitative appendix.

CFG is disabled (guidance scale w=1) to isolate approximation error, but most practical text-to-image editing pipelines use CFG, which the authors themselves note introduces additional, likely larger errors. The transfer of conclusions to realistic settings is not demonstrated.

Some metrics are weak or noisy: FID-10k computed on 20k interpolated samples is statistically fragile; conclusions about 'less manipulative' latent space rely on proxy metrics (SSIM, DreamSim, CLIP similarity) without any human evaluation; the PNG bitrate experiment (table 8) is an unusual and somewhat indirect proxy.

Several observations are model-specific exceptions (e.g., LDM/CelebA shows almost no correlation effect, table 2), suggesting the generality of the findings is weaker than claimed and not fully explained.

strengths: The paper is well-structured around clear research questions, progressing systematically from characterizing the divergence (correlations in DDIM latents), to localizing it (plain/smooth image regions), to explaining its origin (approximation error concentrated in the first ~10% of inversion steps), and finally to a practical mitigation.

Comprehensive empirical coverage: six diverse diffusion models (pixel-space ADMs, LDM, DiT, IF) spanning both conditioned and unconditioned settings, with quantitative metrics (Pearson correlations, variance, PNG bit-rate) and qualitative evidence; the trend appears consistently across architectures.

The proposed solution is simple, cheap (faster by ~4%), and effectively validated: replacing the first 2-4% of inversion steps with forward diffusion removes correlations up to the level of Gaussian noise (Table 7) while preserving reconstruction quality, and yields measurable improvements in interpolation quality (FID/recall) and edit diversity/text alignment (Tables 9-10, 13).

Honest limitations discussion (Appendix A) including the CelebA-HQ exception, dependency on step count, and failure cases; appendix analyses (e.g., behavior at T=1000, noise-to-image mapping, training dynamics) substantially extend the main findings.

The finding that inversion error accumulates disproportionately in the early steps and specifically in plain regions is a useful, actionable insight that connects to recent theory on ODE trajectory curvature and schedule singularities [29, 32].
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core phenomenon: that DDIM inversion latents deviate from Gaussian noise and cause poor editability has already been observed by Parmar et al. [41], Garibi et al. [12], and others; the paper primarily quantifies and localizes a known issue rather than discovering it.

The proposed fix is quite straightforward (forward diffusion of the first few steps, conceptually close to SDEdit-style noising), and its comparison against competing decorrelation/inversion methods is missing - e.g., Renoise [12] (which explicitly regularizes pixel-pair correlations for editability), exact inversion methods [18, 55], or schedule modifications [32]. The method is only compared to naïve DDIM inversion.
The analysis is almost entirely empirical; no theoretical justification is provided for why smooth regions cause higher prediction error, beyond connecting to cited curvature/singularity arguments.

Generality is somewhat undermined by the acknowledged CelebA-HQ exception, and the practical impact evaluation is restricted to interpolation and prompt-based editing; no experiments on standard real-image editing benchmarks (e.g., PIE, EditBench) or with Stable Diffusion-class models in the main text.

Some evaluation choices could bias results toward the conclusion, e.g., PNG bit-rate as a smoothness proxy, and the CLIP-based text alignment analysis is confounded by source/target prompt similarity.

Statistical reporting is inconsistent (some tables lack variance/CI), and there are minor citation errors (e.g., DDIM inversion attributed to Dhariwal and Nichol in places; duplicated Kim et al. references).

strengths: Well-structured analysis paper: the research-question-driven organization (latents vs. noise -> location of latents -> origin of divergence -> consequences and mitigation) makes the empirical narrative easy to follow and the causal chain convincing.

Broad and careful empirical validation across six diverse diffusion models (pixel-space ADMs, latent LDM/DiT, Deepfloyd IF), including both unconditional and conditional settings, with large sample sizes (e.g., N=10k–20k for correlation and interpolation experiments) and a useful ablation over inversion step counts (T=10 to 1000) showing correlations persist even at T=1000.

The tracing of the divergence to the first ~10% of inversion steps, with per-step, per-pixel (plain vs. non-plain) error analysis using cached ground-truth predictions (Sections J, Fig. 4, Table 11), is a genuinely informative diagnostic that connects to existing theory on 1/t curvature blow-up and schedule singularities.

The proposed fix (replacing the first few inversion steps with forward diffusion) is simple, cheap, and empirically effective: it decorrelates latents to near-Gaussian levels while incurring minimal reconstruction cost, and it compares favorably against Pix2Pix-Zero, ReNoise, and DPMSolver-based inversion on a normality/reconstruction/editability/speed trade-off (Table 7).

Honest and thorough limitations discussion (failure cases, LDM/CelebA exception, small-step regime), extensive appendix (noise-image-latent triangle geometry, noise-to-image mapping, training-time evolution), and disclosed compute/LLM usage support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the central findings and the fix: that DDIM inversion latents deviate from Gaussian noise due to approximation error is already acknowledged in prior work (Parmar et al., 2023; Garibi et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024; Wallace et al., 2023), as the authors themselves concede. The fix amounts to partially noising the image (a forward-diffusion to an intermediate step) followed by inversion — an operation closely related to well-known practices (e.g., SDEdit-style stochasticity, partial inversion, Renoise's correlation regularization), so the methodological contribution is incremental even if the analysis justifying *which* steps to replace is new.

Analysis is conducted with classifier-free guidance disabled (w=1), which arguably weakens relevance to the practical text-to-image editing pipelines (SDXL, null-text inversion, etc.) where CFG-induced inversion errors are known to be significant; the editability claims on real images would be more convincing with CFG enabled.
The plain-region identification is a heuristic threshold (τ=0.025 on neighbor differences) with no sensitivity analysis; several conclusions (Tables 3, 5, 11) hinge on this mask definition.

Editing evaluation is modest in scale and scope: 1280 source/target prompts on two models, with diversity metrics measured against source images rather than human judgment or established editing benchmarks; gains in CLIP-T and diversity are consistent but small in absolute terms, and no comparison to state-of-the-art editing methods (only inversion methods) is provided.

Some inconsistencies/rough edges: the abstract ends with a truncated sentence ('code is available a'), and there is tension between claims of 'no increase in reconstruction error' and the measured PSNR drop from 27.58 to 25.68 at the 4% setting in Table 7.

The fix introduces stochasticity, which changes the deterministic character of DDIM inversion — this is framed as a feature (stochastic editing), but for applications requiring reproducible encodings (e.g., consistency, watermarking-style uses of inversion) it is a drawback that is not deeply analyzed.

strengths: The paper is well organized around a clear set of research questions (noise vs. latent differences, origin of divergence, practical consequences), which makes the analysis easy to follow.

The empirical analysis is broad: six different diffusion models (pixel- and latent-space, conditional and unconditional, U-Net and DiT) are examined, and the core observations are validated quantitatively (Pearson correlations, per-region error/variance, KL divergence) rather than only qualitatively.

The attribution of the divergence to the first inversion steps is a useful, well-designed experiment (Eq. 4 and the per-timestep error/variance analysis in Fig. 4 and Table 11), connecting known observations about DDIM inversion errors to the specific structural artifacts in latents (plain regions).

The proposed fix is cheap and simple (a few lines, Algorithm 1), and the paper is honest about the trade-off: it carefully measures reconstruction degradation (Tables 4, 9), evaluates against several existing inversion methods (Table 7), and includes failure cases (Sec. P.1).

The appendix is thorough, covering limitations, compute, and multiple extended experiments (noise-to-image mappings, evolution of noise-image-latent relations over training), which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core observation. That DDIM inversion latents deviate from Gaussian noise and contain image structures has already been noted and partially explained in prior work (Parmar et al., 2023; Garibi et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024; Wallace et al., 2023), which the authors themselves acknowledge. The paper mainly confirms and refines a known phenomenon rather than establishing a fundamentally new insight.

The proposed fix is trivial. Replacing the first inversion steps with a forward diffusion step is essentially equivalent to the well-known SDEdit-style noise-perturbation idea; the main contribution is an empirical demonstration that only ~2-4% of steps need replacing. This is more of an engineering observation than a methodological advance, and it does not address the underlying numerical inversion error at all (which the limitations section admits).

The analysis is almost entirely empirical, with no theory. Connections to known causes of early-step inversion error (1/t curvature blow-up of Lee et al., 2023; schedule singularities of Lin et al., 2024) are cited but not formally developed; the plain-region phenomenon is described, not predicted or characterized analytically.

Most evaluations use self-generated images rather than real images. The editing experiments (Sec. 4.2, Table 6, Fig. 6) primarily invert model-generated samples; real-image editing is shown only qualitatively on a small set of annotated examples (Fig. 13) with GPT-4o annotations, which weakens claims about practical impact on real-image workflows.

Some evaluation choices are unconventional and hard to interpret, e.g., using PNG compressed file size of masked pixels as a proxy for latent diversity (Table 5), and the practical significance of small metric deltas (e.g., CLIP-T changes of ~1-2 points in Table 6/7) is not always convincingly demonstrated.

The comparison to prior inversion methods (Table 7) is on a single model (SDXL) and one benchmark; conclusions about editability trade-offs (e.g., that ReNoise/Pix2Pix-Zero do not improve editability) would need broader validation.

The LDM/CelebA case is an acknowledged exception where the phenomenon largely disappears, suggesting the analysis may not generalize uniformly across data domains, and the explanation offered is speculative.

Significance is moderate: the findings are useful for practitioners doing interpolation/editing with DDIM inversion, but the paper does not change how inversion is done in a fundamental way, and the fix comes at a non-zero reconstruction cost that may matter for editing fidelity-critical applications.

strengths: Well-structured empirical analysis organized around clearly stated research questions, systematically tracing the phenomenon (latent correlations in DDIM inversion) from observation (Sec. 3.1) to localization (Sec. 3.2) to root cause (Sec. 3.3) to practical consequences and mitigation (Sec. 4).

Broad experimental coverage: six diffusion models spanning pixel vs. latent spaces, unconditional vs. conditional (ADM-32/64/256, LDM, DiT, IF), plus SDXL for comparison against prior inversion methods, and models trained from scratch (Appendix O) to track the effect over training time.

The proposed fix is extremely simple (replacing the first 2-4% of inversion steps with forward diffusion), practically free of computational overhead, and the paper convincingly shows it removes latent correlations (Tables 4, 9) while improving interpolation quality/diversity (Fig. 5) and editability (Tables 6, 7, Fig. 7) with minimal reconstruction degradation.

Comprehensive head-to-head comparison with existing inversion methods (Pix2Pix-Zero, ReNoise, DPMSolver-based inversion) on normality, reconstruction, prompt alignment, and speed (Table 7), showing the fix achieves the best trade-off.

Extensive and transparent appendix (limitations, compute resources, pseudocode, failure cases, additional studies such as noise-to-image l2 mapping and training dynamics), plus code availability, supporting reproducibility.

The mechanistic attribution — that early inversion steps produce erroneous and insufficiently diverse noise predictions for smooth/plain image regions — extends prior analyses (Lee et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024) in a way that is directly actionable.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the fact that DDIM inversion latents deviate from Gaussian noise has already been reported in prior works (Parmar et al., 2023; Garibi et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024), and the paper itself positions this as validating/consolidating existing observations. The genuinely new contributions are the region-level (plain vs. non-plain) attribution and the simple fix, which are relatively incremental.

The analysis is largely empirical; there is little formal/theoretical treatment of why the early-step error concentrates on smooth regions (only connections to prior curvature/singularity arguments are sketched). A more rigorous characterization of the error propagation would strengthen the paper.

Some quantitative evidence is weaker than the narrative: the diversity/alignment improvements in Table 6 and Table 12 are modest in absolute terms (e.g., DreamSim 0.68 vs. 0.71 for DiT), and no human evaluation is provided to confirm that the interpolated/edited outputs are perceptually better; several conclusions rest on FID/Recall and CLIP-based metrics alone.

Inconsistencies and under-explained results raise questions: e.g., in Table 6 the CLIP-T(PS) for IF latent (0.649) is dramatically higher than noise (0.273) while DiT shows the opposite trend, with no explanation; the LDM/CelebA exception is only briefly discussed; some trend reversals in Table 9 (e.g., 'w/ our fix 0.2%' KL lower than '1%') are not addressed.

The fix fundamentally changes the nature of inversion: injecting random noise breaks determinism, so reconstruction is no longer an inverse of the generation process and stochasticity varies per seed. While the paper frames this as enabling stochastic editing, the trade-off semantics (reproducibility of the latent-to-image mapping) deserve deeper discussion, particularly for applications relying on deterministic latent geometry.

Practical validation on real images is comparatively thin: most quantitative experiments use model-generated (sampled) images where the ground-truth noise is known; the real-image editing examples (Fig. 13, ImageNet-R-TI2I) are qualitative only, and evaluation of reconstruction error on real images (the most common use case) is not clearly separated.

A minor but noticeable issue: the abstract ends mid-sentence ('The code is available a'), and several figures/tables in the main text rely heavily on appendix details, which slightly hampers self-containedness and polish.
